items.readable_text:
Content:
Line integrals of vector-valued functions share a fundamental connection with line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.]

Content:
Consider a vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] on [MATH: \mathbb R^2] with components [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j]

Content:
Now suppose that [MATH: C] is a smooth curve on [MATH: \mathbb R^2,] given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].]

Content:
Then, we can write the line integral of [MATH: \mathbf F] along [MATH: C] as

Content:
[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_{a}^{b}F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}(P(x(t), y(t))i + Q(x(t), y(t))j) ⋅ ((dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j)dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}(P(x(t), y(t))(dx)/(dt) + Q(x(t), y(t))(dy)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}P(x(t), y(t))(dx)/(dt)dt + Q(x(t), y(t))(dy)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}P(x, y)dx + Q(x, y)dy.]

Content:
So, we have the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = \int_a^b P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y) \,\textrm d y]

Content:
An analogous result holds for vector fields on [MATH: \mathbb R^3.] That is,

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = \int_a^b P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z) \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Since there is a fundamental link between line integrals of vector-valued functions and line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] it should be unsurprising that they share similar properties. We list two of them below:

Content:
- If [MATH: -C] denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of [MATH: C,] then
[MATH: \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.]
- If [MATH: C = C_1\cup C_2] is the union of two paths [MATH: C_1] and [MATH: C_2], then
[MATH: \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.]

Content:
The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] and the line segment [MATH: \overline{AB},] shown below. Let [MATH: C] be the path defined by traversing the line segment from [MATH: A] to [MATH: B.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/94572df4ae212a603ac63748df659358]

Content:
Let [MATH: W(C)] be the work done in moving the particle along [MATH: C.] Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have
[MATH: W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.]

Content:
However, if we move the particle from [MATH: B] to [MATH: A,] we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against [MATH: \mathbf F.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/98d2a57d73d03a14fcd016d9b495fab5]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.]

Content:
We can show that the work done in moving the particle along [MATH: -C] is the same as the work done in moving it along [MATH: C] but with the opposite sign. That is

Content:
[MATH: W(-C) = -W(C).]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Line integrals of vector-valued functions share a fundamental connection with line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.]

Content:
Consider a vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] on [MATH: \mathbb R^2] with components [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j]

Content:
Now suppose that [MATH: C] is a smooth curve on [MATH: \mathbb R^2,] given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].]

Content:
Then, we can write the line integral of [MATH: \mathbf F] along [MATH: C] as

Content:
[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_{a}^{b}F(r(t)) ⋅ r^{′}(t)dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}(P(x(t), y(t))i + Q(x(t), y(t))j) ⋅ ((dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j)dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}(P(x(t), y(t))(dx)/(dt) + Q(x(t), y(t))(dy)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}P(x(t), y(t))(dx)/(dt)dt + Q(x(t), y(t))(dy)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}P(x, y)dx + Q(x, y)dy.]

Content:
So, we have the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = \int_a^b P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y) \,\textrm d y]

Content:
An analogous result holds for vector fields on [MATH: \mathbb R^3.] That is,

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r = \int_a^b P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z) \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y) = (3x+2) \: \mathbf{i} - y^3 \: \mathbf{j}] and let [MATH: C] be a path in [MATH: \mathbb R^2.] Write [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}] in the form [MATH: \displaystyle\int_a^b P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)\,\textrm d y.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given a piecewise-smooth path [MATH: C] and a vector field
[MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y) = P(x,y) \: \mathbf{i} + Q(x,y) \: \mathbf{j}]

defined on [MATH: C,] we have
[MATH: \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_C P(x,y) \: \text{d}x + Q(x,y) \: \text{d}y.]

In our case, [MATH: P = 3x+2] and [MATH: Q = -y^3.] Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_(C)(3x + 2)dx − y^{3}dy.]

---

Choices:

Item 5 — Tutorial: Reversing the Orientation of a Curve and Sums Over Unions of Paths

Content:
Since there is a fundamental link between line integrals of vector-valued functions and line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] it should be unsurprising that they share similar properties. We list two of them below:

Content:
- If [MATH: -C] denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of [MATH: C,] then
[MATH: \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.]
- If [MATH: C = C_1\cup C_2] is the union of two paths [MATH: C_1] and [MATH: C_2], then
[MATH: \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.]

Content:
The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field [MATH: \mathbf F] and the line segment [MATH: \overline{AB},] shown below. Let [MATH: C] be the path defined by traversing the line segment from [MATH: A] to [MATH: B.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/94572df4ae212a603ac63748df659358]

Content:
Let [MATH: W(C)] be the work done in moving the particle along [MATH: C.] Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have
[MATH: W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.]

Content:
However, if we move the particle from [MATH: B] to [MATH: A,] we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against [MATH: \mathbf F.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/98d2a57d73d03a14fcd016d9b495fab5]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.]

Content:
We can show that the work done in moving the particle along [MATH: -C] is the same as the work done in moving it along [MATH: C] but with the opposite sign. That is

Content:
[MATH: W(-C) = -W(C).]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/4c07015f012adfb9c576718541a44fe8]

Consider the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},] where [MATH: C] is the closed polygonal path [MATH: FGHF] shown above, traversed in the clockwise direction. Express this integral as a sum of line integrals along [MATH: C_1, C_2,] and [MATH: C_3.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that we can represent [MATH: C,] which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of [MATH: 3] paths:

[MATH: C = \{-C_1\} \cup \{-C_2\} \cup C_3,]

where [MATH: -C_1] and [MATH: -C_2] are the same paths as [MATH: C_1] and [MATH: C_2] but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_(− C_{1})F ⋅ dr + ∫_(− C_{2})F ⋅ dr + ∫_(C_{3})F ⋅ dr; = − ∫_(C_{1})F ⋅ dr − ∫_(C_{2})F ⋅ dr + ∫_(C_{3})F ⋅ dr.]

Item 9 — Example: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/962f5b7322eaec11b61a09faa7e19175]

The path [MATH: C_1] consists of a line segment from the point [MATH: A(-2,0)] to the point [MATH: O(0,0),] and the path [MATH: C_2] consists of a line segment from the point [MATH: O(0,0)] to the point [MATH: B(1,1).]

Given that [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = -4,] evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},] where [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (2y-5x)\,\mathbf {j}] and [MATH: C = C_1\cup C_2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We will use the fact that
[MATH: \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}.]

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path [MATH: C_2] is the line segment from [MATH: O] to [MATH: B.] It can be parametrized as
[MATH: r_{2}(t)|= b + t(c − b); = ⟨0, 0⟩ + t(⟨1, 1⟩ − ⟨0, 0⟩); = ⟨t, t⟩; = ti + tj,]
where [MATH: 0 \lt t \lt 1.] Along this segment, we have [MATH: x = t] and [MATH: y = t.] Therefore,
[MATH: F(r_{2}(t))|= (2x − 3y)i + (2y − 5x)j; = (2t − 3t)i + (2t − 5t)j; = − ti − 3tj.]

Computing the derivative, we get the following:
[MATH: r_{2}^{′}(t)|= (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)(t)j; = i + j]

We can now compute the dot product:
[MATH: F(r_{2}(t)) ⋅ r_{2}^{′}(t)|= (− ti − 3tj) ⋅ (i + j); = − t ⋅ 1 + (− 3t) ⋅ 1; = − 4t]

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)F ⋅ dr|= ∫_(C_{1})F ⋅ dr + ∫_(C_{2})F ⋅ dr; = − 4 + ∫_{0}^{1}F(r_{2}(t)) ⋅ r_{2}^{′}(t)dt; = − 4 + ∫_{0}^{1}(− 4t)dt; = − 4 + [− 2t^{2}]_{0}^{1}; = − 4 + [− 2 + 0]; = − 6]
